analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes the Endangered Species Act while narrowing protections for threatened and endangered species.
analysis.headline: The House has not yet voted on a bill that reauthorizes the Endangered Species Act through 2031 while narrowing species protections, though it cleared committee on a 25-16 party-line vote and a floor rule was reported.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend federal funding for the Endangered Species Act for six more years while rewriting parts of the law to make protecting species harder. It removes the current rule that the government must decide within a year whether a species should be listed as endangered, narrows which land can be protected as critical habitat, lets states take over protecting threatened species within their borders, and exempts permits to harm or kill protected species from environmental review. It also caps attorney fees for groups that sue over ESA decisions and limits how effects of a project on a species are judged. Supporters say these changes cut red tape and reward landowners for voluntary conservation; opponents say they weaken protections that have prevented extinctions for fifty years.
analysis.who_benefits: Private landowners, and the industries that operate on or develop land — mining, oil and gas, timber, and real estate — gain the most. The bill limits what land can be called critical habitat, narrows how agencies judge harm to species, exempts take permits from environmental review, guarantees landowners no new restrictions if a species is later listed, and makes it harder for conservation groups to recover attorney fees when they sue. States also gain new authority to manage threatened species recovery themselves.

how_it_helps.text: Reauthorizes ESA funding at roughly $288 million per year for the Fish and Wildlife Service through fiscal 2031, plus companion accounts, giving conservation programs a dedicated funding schedule.

Creates statutory Conservation Benefit Agreements: private landowners voluntarily reduce threats to at-risk species in exchange for a guarantee that no new land, water, or resource use restrictions will be imposed on them if the species is later listed.

Exempts incidental take permits and their conservation agreements from National Environmental Policy Act review, and limits 'reasonable and prudent measures' so agencies cannot require mitigation offsets — shortening and simplifying permitting.

Lets a state, if the Fish and Wildlife Service approves, use its own recovery strategy as the rule for protecting a threatened species within that state, and allows state-regulated management of threatened species.

Requires agencies to publish the scientific basis for listing and critical-habitat decisions online and to disclose litigation costs in a public database — transparency provisions that apply to any administration.

analysis.who_pays: If it becomes law, the cost falls on the species themselves and on the public interest in preventing extinction: listing decisions could wait years, critical habitat designations could be more easily avoided, state management could replace federal protections for threatened species, and the public loses environmental review of permits to harm or kill listed species. People who use public lands and waters for recreation or depend on healthy ecosystems also bear indirect costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the legal requirement to act within 12 months on petitions to list a species, and its new priority system lets the Secretary hold low-priority species in a work plan for years — species can wait through delays with no deadline for a decision.

It exempts incidental take permits — permits to harm or kill a listed species — from environmental review under NEPA, removing the public's opportunity to review the impacts before such permits are issued.

It narrows critical habitat by defining 'habitat' to exclude areas outside a species' current or historic range, limiting protection for species whose habitat is shifting, and it blocks designation of critical habitat on privately owned land covered by a qualifying land-management plan.

It limits attorney fee awards to smaller organizations and caps total fees at $200,000 per suit, which reduces the ability of citizen groups to challenge weak listing or protection decisions in court.
It bars judicial review of delisting decisions during the post-delisting monitoring period and channels other review challenges to a single court, narrowing oversight of species removal decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real, narrow benefits: predictable timelines, binding conservation commitments from landowners, and public disclosure of how ESA money and lawsuits are spent. But the heart of the bill is a rollback — it removes the deadline for listing decisions, narrows critical habitat, allows states to take over protections for threatened species, and waives environmental review for permits to harm or kill listed species. The cost of slower protections is borne by species that can decline past recovery, and the benefits of weaker consultation rules flow mostly to businesses that want to develop or extract on sensitive land. For ordinary people, the trade is less tangible: cleaner, intact ecosystems and working public conservation law versus marginally faster permits. On balance the drawbacks outweigh the benefits for anyone who does not directly hold a stake in land or resource use.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Natural Resources Committee on a 25-16 vote in December 2025, was reported to the House in March 2026, and a rule setting up floor debate was reported in April 2026 — but the House has not voted on it yet.

narrative.text: Introduced March 6, 2025, by Rep. Bruce Westerman with 16 Republican original cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
After a subcommittee hearing in March 2025, the subcommittee was discharged and the full committee marked the bill up on December 17, 2025, ordering it reported as amended on a 25-16 vote.
The committee reported the amended bill on March 24, 2026 (H. Rept. 119-568), and it was placed on the Union Calendar.

On April 20, 2026, the Rules Committee reported a closed rule providing one hour of debate and one motion to recommit for H.R. 1897, meaning the bill could come to the House floor but no floor amendments would be allowed.
As of the latest action in the record, the House has not taken a final vote on the bill, and the Senate has not acted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has fully won: the bill's supporters have moved it to the edge of a floor vote, while opponents have delayed it for over a year. If it passes and becomes law, resource industries and landowners stand to gain; if it stalls, endangered species keep current protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — bill is unenacted

sides.party_line_note: All 27 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans, and the committee voted to report the bill 25-16 with the Republican majority in favor; no Democrats appear as supporters in the record.

industries.industry: Private landowners and real estate/development interests
industries.note: The bill guarantees that landowners who sign conservation agreements face no new restrictions if a species is later listed, narrows what land can be designated critical habitat, and lets land-management plans block habitat designations. It protects property use and value at the possible expense of species recovery.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and other resource-extraction industries
industries.note: Narrowing what counts as an effect on a species, limiting consultation measures, allowing successive consultations to be discontinued, and exempting take permits from environmental review all reduce the regulatory hurdles for projects on or near endangered-species habitat.

Some litigation costs are capped at $200,000 and fees limited to eligible smaller parties, making it harder for advocacy groups to fund challenges; delisting decisions during monitoring are shielded from judicial review. On the other side, the bill adds public databases of lawsuit spending and online publication of the science behind listings.
States gain authority to run their own recovery strategies for threatened species and state data must be weighed in listing decisions, shifting power from federal agencies to state governments.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a floor rule and sits on the House calendar, so a House vote is likely soon; with a 223-seat Republican majority it would probably pass the House, as a similar bill did in the previous Congress. It would then face a harder path in the closely divided Senate, where bills weakening species protections have historically stalled.
